title: Linear programming: simplex vs ellipsoid / interior-point methods
problem_statement: Given A in Q^(m x n), b in Q^m, c in Q^n, maximise c^T x subject to Ax <= b, x >= 0 (or report infeasible / unbounded).

input.parameter: n variables, m constraints; L = total bit length of (A, b, c).

algorithms.name: simplex method (Dantzig's pivot rule)
algorithms.idea: Walk along edges of the feasible polytope from vertex to vertex, never decreasing the objective.
algorithms.time_complexity: exponential in the worst case: 2^n - 1 pivots on the Klee-Minty cube
algorithms.correctness: Dantzig 1951; termination with anti-cycling rules (e.g. Bland's rule).

algorithms.name: ellipsoid method
algorithms.idea: Maintain an ellipsoid containing the optimum region; cut it in half with a violated constraint and replace it by a smaller enclosing ellipsoid.
algorithms.time_complexity: polynomial in n and L: O(n^2 L) iterations of O(n^2) arithmetic operations

algorithms.name: interior-point method (Karmarkar)
algorithms.idea: Move through the interior of the polytope along projective-scaled steepest-descent directions.

relationship: Simplex (with the classical pivot rules) is exponential in the worst case; ellipsoid and interior-point methods are polynomial in the input bit length L.

sources.title: Maximization of a linear function of variables subject to linear inequalities
sources.venue: Activity Analysis of Production and Allocation (T. C. Koopmans, ed.), Wiley, 339-347

sources.title: How good is the simplex algorithm?
sources.venue: Inequalities III (O. Shisha, ed.), Academic Press, 159-175

sources.title: A polynomial algorithm in linear programming
sources.venue: Doklady Akademii Nauk SSSR 244(5), 1093-1096 (English: Soviet Mathematics Doklady 20, 191-194)

sources.title: A new polynomial-time algorithm for linear programming
Smoothed analysis of algorithms: Why the simplex algorithm usually takes polynomial time

verification.method: Cited from the literature; not independently implemented.

caveats: Ellipsoid and interior-point methods are WEAKLY polynomial (polynomial in L, not only in n and m). Whether LP has a STRONGLY polynomial algorithm is open (Smale's 9th problem), hence secondary tag T6. Whether some simplex pivot rule is polynomial is also open. In practice simplex is fast; smoothed analysis (Spielman-Teng) explains part of this.
notes: Not implemented; the costs are as stated in the cited sources.
